subject: The Papyrus · The dam that ended the flood
html:
For 5,000 years the Nile flooded. Then it stopped.

Every summer for millennia, the Nile rose and spilled across its valley, leaving the black silt that made Egyptian agriculture possible — and sometimes drowning villages, sometimes failing to come at all. The Aswan High Dam, built 1960–1970, ended that ancient rhythm on purpose. It stands about 111 metres high with a crest nearly 3,830 metres long, and behind it sits Lake Nasser, one of the largest reservoirs on earth. (Source: Britannica.)

A dam that was also a Cold War

Its story is as much politics as engineering. When Western financing was withdrawn in the 1950s, the Soviet Union stepped in to finance and help build it — and Nasser's move to nationalise the Suez Canal to help fund the project helped trigger the 1956 Suez Crisis. The dam gave Egypt year-round irrigation and a large share of its electricity, and it became the symbol of the modern republic.

But every big number has a cost column. Ending the flood also ended the free annual silt, so Egypt's farmland now leans on fertiliser (which loops back to the fertiliser prices on our own site); the Nubian heartland was submerged and its people resettled; the temples of Abu Simbel had to be cut apart and lifted to higher ground. Progress and loss in the same reservoir — which is exactly why you read the whole ledger, not just the headline.
